title: The world before Nanak
hook: his first var describes a dark age of empty ritual and quarrels over labels, before Nanak came

segments.voice: Yesterday, kunji, the key: tradition's name for Bhai Gurdas's vars, which open a door and step aside. Today we use the key for the first time.

Truth, left standing on the bank, while two men quarrel themselves to ruin. That's one of the pictures Bhai Gurdas paints in his first var, before Guru Nanak has even been born into the story. Before the hero walks on, the storyteller shows what's wrong with the world he walks into, and he doesn't go easy. Today: kalyug.
screen: `TRUTH, LEFT ON THE BANK.` → `SETTING THE STAGE.` → `THE WORLD BEFORE NANAK.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas calls it the kalyug, the dark age. And look at what he says is dark. Not a lack of religion; there's plenty of religion in his picture. People divided into castes on one side and into rival schools on the other. Hindus heading for the Ganges and Banaras, Muslims for Mecca and the Kaaba. One side proud of the sacred thread and the forehead mark, the other of its own outward signs. Both call on God, Ram for some, Rahim for others, and Bhai Gurdas says it's one Name, but they lose their way on two roads. Pride, stubbornness and quarreling fill the space where devotion should be. Then the line from the hook: truth stood off on the bank while the Brahmin and the maulvi wore each other out. Hear this carefully, because it's easy to mishear. Bhai Gurdas isn't attacking Hindus, or Muslims, or their scriptures. In the same passage he says people forgot what their own books taught. His target is what happens when a label, a mark or a place of pilgrimage becomes the whole of faith, and the people under the labels stop seeing each other. He is painting a mood in the world, not grading anyone's religion. That's the darkness: ritual with nobody home, and neighbors turned rivals over names for the same God. Then, at the end of the stretch, the turn. Bhai Gurdas says the generous Lord heard the cry of the world, and sent Guru Nanak into it. The light comes tomorrow.
screen: `THE KALYUG: A DARK AGE.` · `PLENTY OF RELIGION, LITTLE TRUTH.` · `ONE NAME, TWO ROADS, ONE QUARREL.` · `THE CRY IS HEARD.` · then, large: `BEFORE THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Find one habit you go through with nobody home, not necessarily a religious one: saying "fine" when someone asks how you are, scrolling the same three apps before you get out of bed, a thank you said without looking up. Don't scold yourself; just sit with it and ask what it was once meant to be for. If you pray, you can ask for that one thing to be filled again.
Kalyug, the dark age Bhai Gurdas pictures in his first var: labels, quarrels and empty ritual, with truth left standing on the bank, until the cry was heard.
Your line: before the light. The stage is set, and the cry has been heard. That's day six hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Bhai Gurdas's first var hear its opening stanzas as the backdrop to Guru Nanak's coming: a world where outward signs and rivalries had crowded out devotion to the one Name.

fork.setup: you're a poet about to tell the life of Guru Nanak. before he arrives, how do you describe the world?
options: a golden age that only needed polishing.
a dark age, full of religion, quarreling over labels.
a world that had never heard of God.
fork.reveal: Bhai Gurdas paints a world crowded with pilgrimages, marks and rival schools, where people called on one Name and lost their way on two roads.

trapdoor: what you thought: the world before Nanak was a world without faith.
what it means: in Bhai Gurdas's picture, faith had shrunk to labels, places and marks, and people fought over them.
what a scholar hears: he names Hindus and Muslims side by side, in matching lines, so the darkness belongs to no single community.

the seventh Guru, a gentle healer
guess: the dark age, when ritual and quarrels crowded out truth

chat.says: Your lesson called it a dark age. Was Bhai Gurdas saying the other religions were wrong?
options: No; he says people forgot their own books, and labels and quarrels left truth on the bank.
Yes; he says Hindu and Muslim scriptures had gone dark and needed replacing.
No; he says the dark age meant there was hardly any religion left at all.
chat.meaning: Bhai Gurdas says people forgot what their own books taught; his target is labels and quarrels crowding out truth, not anyone's scripture.

kalyug.meaning: the dark age, in Bhai Gurdas's picture

Banaras.meaning: a holy Hindu city on the Ganges

Kaaba.meaning: the sacred house at the center of Mecca

Rahim.meaning: the Merciful, a Muslim name for God

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 21 (four castes, four schools; truth left on the bank)
Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 23 (the cry heard; Guru Nanak sent)
